paragraphs.source_en: Although Round Head motifs are rather limited in number and are repetitive, they nevertheless reveal important information. The main and perhaps decisive factor in determining this artistic tradition is the representation of specific animals as probable climatic and cultural indicators. The climatic changes which occurred in the past 20,000 years in the Sahara conditioned the appearance and disappearance of those animal species closely dependent on large quantities of water. Some of these animals, such as hippopotamus and elephant, are represented in the Round Head art. Other animals depicted, namely antelope and mouflon, may be directly related to the archaeological record of sites excavated in the study area. By unifying pieces of information from various fields (rock art, zoology, archaeology and climatology) a better chronological picture begins to emerge.

paragraphs.source_en: The most represented fauna, namely antelope and mouflon, are able to live in dry environments and they are extremely resistant to desert conditions, so that they are not suitable as climatic indicators. Among the faunal remains in the Early Holocene layers of excavated sites, mouflon is the predominant animal which indicates that it also lived during a very humid climate (Barich 1987; Cremaschi & Di Lernia 1996b). This important aspect, namely the same preponderance of mouflon in the rock art and within the material record, is not accidental and it will be examined later.

paragraphs.source_en: Other animals depicted in the Round Head art are bovids. The biological family Bovidae includes several diverse groups, including domestic cattle. It is difficult to determine the exact species from the paintings but according to the shape of the horns these are likely to be Pelorovis antiquus, a genus of African wild cattle which have been extinct since around 5,000 BP (Barnett & Mattingly 2003) and Syncerus caffer, the African buffalo. These animals depend on water and therefore they are good indicators of a wet climate. Other paintings of bovids have different shaped horns which resemble wildebeests (Connochaetes gnou; Connochaetes taurinus) and hartebeests (Alcelaphus buselaphus). Wildebeests are also water dependant whilst hartebeests are more resistant to drier environmental conditions (Estes 1991).
